item.title: Secret documents reveal donors behind $330 million for Trump's ballroom
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member. Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million, the top contribution amount, the list shows. The Adelson family, one of the GOP’s largest donor dynasties, committed that sum as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Absent from the list is Trump himself, who has said that he is helping to pay for the project. “It’s being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine,” he said last year, days after demolition began on the old East Wing. The White House publicly identified 37 people, companies and foundations as donors last October, without revealing the amount of their individual gifts. The list obtained by The Post, an internal spreadsheet used to track contributions for the fundraising effort, contains the source, date and amount of all 67 donations above $10,000 recorded as of late last month. It shows a total of $333 million from private donors, aligning with the administration’s public statements. Additional records, also internal to the fundraising effort, provide more detail about the donations and indicate that at least $77 million came from donors who requested anonymity. The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls. Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving. Some donors on the list obtained by The Post cut large checks, while others created installment plans that are still being paid off, the additional records show. The list does not include in-kind contributions. The Post’s reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government. Companies or executives of firms that have had contracts with the federal government during Trump’s second term accounted for about half of the total, The Post found. After reviewing the list obtained by The Post, White House spokesman Davis Ingle declined to discuss individual donations but described the ballroom donors as “a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People’s House better for generations to come.” “The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations,” he said. He added that the administration will “relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give.” The Post is publishing the names of the 57 donors listed as having committed to giving $100,000 or more. The additional records detailing donors’ preferences show at least nine wanted to remain anonymous. The Post attempted to reach all the donors whose names appear in this report. Most did not respond or declined to comment. Those who did comment said that there was no connection between their donations and any favorable government actions. Nvidia, the world’s most valuable public company, became a top contributor to the ballroom in October 2025, nearly three months after it struck a groundbreaking pact with Trump to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns. CEO Jensen Huang told reporters at the time that the company was contributing to Trump’s ballroom “in a small way” but did not provide a dollar amount. Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous. “As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in response to questions from The Post. “We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made.” Major GOP donor Joseph Popolo Jr., Trump’s ambassador to the Netherlands, and his wife contributed $1 million from their family fund to support the ballroom project in late 2025, the records show. Their donation - made two months after Popolo’s confirmation - has not been previously reported. Trump Cabinet member Kelly Loeffler of the Small Business Administration and her husband Jeff Sprecher, former chairman of the New York Stock Exchange, promised $5 million for the project, the list shows. Brandon Lutnick, chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald and the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, donated stock worth more than $2.5 million, the records show. Popolo, Loeffler, Sprecher and the Lutnicks did not respond to requests for comment. More than three-quarters of the money for the ballroom came in commitments of $5 million or more. Among the top donors are some of America’s blue-chip companies, including Amazon, Caterpillar, Comcast, Microsoft and T-Mobile. (Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos owns The Post . ) Cryptocurrency companies, now under loosened regulations from the Trump administration, and their investors promised more than $18 million. The largest portion came from Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss, co-founders of the Gemini crypto exchange, who together donated bitcoin valued at $5,050,018, the records show. The Winklevoss brothers did not respond to requests for comment. The ballroom project has also received dozens of small contributions, some as low as $10. The list and additional documents show the source of all but $24,000 of the total donations. The total fundraising amount falls short of the $400 million Trump has said he intends to raise for the work. The cost of building the new East Wing, which includes the ballroom, office space and an underground military facility, was projected in March to have increased to $600 million, an estimate previously reported by The Post. The White House has used taxpayer dollars to cover some of the construction cost, records show. The ballroom donations are routed through the Trust for the National Mall, a D.C.-based nonprofit whose mission is to restore and preserve the National Mall and the White House grounds. Nonprofits are not generally required to disclose their donors. Prospective donors were sent a “pledge agreement form,” a copy of which was obtained by The Post, for giving toward the “Donald J. Trump Ballroom.” The form lists Meredith O’Rourke, the top fundraiser for Trump’s 2024 campaign, as the main contact. O’Rourke referred questions to the White House. A 12-page agreement between the government and the Trust requires that the Trust “maintain the anonymity of Project donors to the extent provided by law and not publicly recognize any such donor unless explicitly authorized in writing” by staff in the White House’s Executive Residence unit. Democratic lawmakers have denounced the fundraising for the ballroom as secretive and potentially transactional. They have demanded that the administration and the Trust provide details about the donors and circumstances of the gifts. Those demands have been rebuffed. In a statement the Trust said: “In philanthropy, it is not uncommon for donors to request their gifts remain anonymous. The Trust is committed to honoring donors requesting anonymity.” Pardon for international banker One of the earliest commitments to donate to the ballroom, from Sept. 23, 2025, came from the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, an international banker and dual Venezuelan-Italian citizen. In 2022, the Justice Department indicted Herrera Velutini, then 50, on bribery charges, accusing him of helping finance the campaign of Puerto Rico’s then-governor in exchange for the removal of a regulator investigating his bank. The former governor and a political consultant were also charged. Herrera Velutini and his attorney unsuccessfully tried to get the case dismissed, claiming prosecutors were criminalizing lawful political activity. After Trump’s victory, Herrera’s daughter, Isabela Herrera, made two donations to Trump’s MAGA Inc., a political action committee, totaling $3.5 million, campaign finance records show. The donations prompted the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center to file a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging that Isabela Herrera was serving as a “straw donor” for her father. The organization described her as a self-employed financial consultant in her mid-20s whose only prior political donation was $20 to Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate. The organization said it got no response from the FEC, which declined to comment for this story. In August 2025, Herrera Velutini’s charges were reduced to a misdemeanor as part of a plea agreement. The following month, Isabela Herrera committed to donating $2.5 million for the ballroom, which has not been previously reported. Records show she paid a first installment of $835,000 on Oct. 14, 2025. Trump pardoned Herrera Velutini in January. Herrera’s second payment was due this month, the records show. Amid a wider Justice Department retreat from sweeping public corruption investigations, Trump also pardoned the former governor and the political consultant. The White House said the prosecutions had been politically motivated. After the pardon, an attorney for Herrera Velutini issued a statement saying his client was “profoundly grateful to President Donald J. Trump for bestowing the grace of his benevolent pardon.” Neither Herrera Velutini nor his daughter responded to requests for comment. A dropped investigation Last year, Ergen, the telecommunications executive, found his company EchoStar in the Trump administration’s crosshairs. Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, wrote Ergen in May to inform him that the agency had begun investigating EchoStar. Carr threatened to yank government licenses that were critical to the survival of the business, accusing EchoStar, owner of Dish Network, of not following through on promises it had made to upgrade its cellphone network. The following month, Ergen met with Trump and Carr behind closed doors to discuss the investigation, according to Bloomberg. The outlet, citing unnamed sources, said the June 11 discussion included a brief exchange about Ergen’s political donations and whether he gave to candidates in both political parties. The company referenced a June 11 meeting between Ergen and Carr in a regulatory filing and wrote that Trump “subsequently encouraged the parties involved to reach an amicable resolution.” Ergen negotiated a deal to sell some of the company’s licenses to AT&T in August, subject to approval of the FCC and Justice Department. Carr dropped the investigation the following month, thanking Ergen for his responses and for information he had provided. In December, with the sale still pending, Ergen committed $12.5 million to Trump’s ballroom, according to the donation list. Records indicate Ergen requested that the source of the donation remain anonymous. The donation has not been previously reported. He committed another $12.5 million in February, according to the list. In May, the FCC and the Justice Department each gave EchoStar approval for the sale. Through a spokesman, Ergen and EchoStar declined to comment. The FCC and Carr did not respond. DOJ did not provide comment for this story. The donor list also shows $5 million “pledged” by AT&T, the only line item on the list described that way. Every other amount is listed as “won.” In a statement to The Post, AT&T spokesperson Megan Ketterer said the company appeared to have been listed in error. “We have no idea what list you are talking about and have no plans to contribute to the Trust for the National Mall,” Ketterer said. An approval, then a donation Another top donor was a subsidiary of Rocket, the Detroit-based housing, finance and tech company founded by Daniel Gilbert, owner of the NBA’s Cleveland Cavaliers. In March 2025, Rocket said that it planned to acquire two competitors: the home search site Redfin and the mortgage site Mr. Cooper. The moves would give Rocket a much larger share of the real estate market. Federal agencies tasked with protecting against anticompetitive business practices declined to challenge the deals, allowing them to proceed. Five Democratic senators wrote to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission in protest. To acquire Mr. Cooper, Gilbert also needed approval from the Federal Housing Finance Agency. The FHFA approved the deal on Aug. 26, 2025. The Rocket subsidiary committed $10 million to the ballroom three weeks later. Records show it requested anonymity. A Rocket spokesperson said the approvals and donation were not connected. “Rocket and its related companies have supported the Trust for the National Mall and other nonpartisan organizations in Washington for more than a decade,” said spokesperson Aaron Emerson. “We’re proud to join dozens of companies and individuals in improving our nation’s capital.” An FTC spokesperson said Rocket received no special treatment, pointing to a lawsuit the agency brought against Redfin for anticompetitive practices days after the donation. The FHFA and the Justice Department did not provide comment. Software contracts One of the country’s leading software providers, Salesforce, has significantly grown its government contracting business during the second Trump administration. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has attended exclusive dinners and events with Trump, including a state dinner hosted by King Charles III at Windsor Castle in September 2025 and a business summit in Japan the following month. While there, Trump thanked Benioff for previously putting him on the cover of Time magazine, which Benioff owns. “Marc has some pretty good suggestions,” Trump said of the CEO. The following day, Benioff committed $1 million to the ballroom, according to the list. The donation has not previously been reported, and Benioff asked that it remain anonymous. Salesforce separately made two $1 million commitments to the ballroom, one last Christmas Eve and another Jan. 29 of this year, the list shows. The donations have not been previously reported. In between, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $5.6 billion through 2035, which appears to be the largest public government contract in Salesforce’s history, according to a review of public contracting records. Announcing the contract, the Pentagon said “bids were solicited via the internet with only one received.” Benioff and Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment. In a statement, a Pentagon official said: “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.” After this article published, an Army spokesperson said in a statement that contracts are awarded in strict compliance with federal law and are “determined exclusively by validated mission requirements, technical capability, and best value.” One of Salesforce’s competitors, ServiceNow, also donated to the ballroom. Last September, the General Services Administration announced what it called a “landmark” agreement with ServiceNow that would make the company’s AI-driven software available to federal agencies at a discount. “When President Trump says the federal government needs to operate like a best-run business, he means it,” CEO Bill McDermott said as part of the announcement. The next month, ServiceNow committed $5 million to the ballroom, a donation that has not been previously reported. The GSA said in a statement that ServiceNow has been a federal contractor for more than a decade, adding that “its charitable or political donations - like those of any company - have no bearing on GSA’s decision to include them in federal buying catalogs.” ServiceNow said in a statement that negotiations for the deal had been underway for a “considerable period of time.” Its government business is “separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause,” it said. Of the donation, the company said: “Many of our partners and peers were also contributing to the project. We chose to join them.” Venezuelan oil interests Nearly $10 million for the ballroom was committed by two Trump political donors who have pursued large investments in Venezuelan oil - a market Trump has gained influence over since the U.S. seizure of President Nicolás Maduro in January. Billionaire financier Paul Singer committed to donate $5 million through his foundation in October 2025, a month before his hedge fund received court approval to pursue a purchase of Venezuelan oil giant Citgo for $5.9 billion. The deal will require approval from multiple federal agencies, including the Commerce Department, Energy Department, State Department and Treasury Department. It has stalled amid ongoing negotiations with the South American country’s U.S.-backed administration. The Oklahoma oil and gas company Continental Resources and its chairman emeritus, billionaire and GOP megadonor Harold Hamm, both promised donations to the ballroom in October 2025 totaling just under $5 million. This year, in response to the Trump administration’s call for energy companies to invest in the Venezuelan oil industry, Continental struck a tentative agreement with the country’s state-run oil company to develop 126,000 acres of untapped oil fields. Singer declined to comment. Neither Hamm nor Continental responded. Unlisted Two companies and one individual the White House has publicly named as donors do not appear on the list obtained by The Post. The companies are Hard Rock International, the hospitality chain owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and Tether America, a cryptocurrency firm. The individual is Paolo Tiramani, a modular homes company executive who told the Times of London that he had donated $10 million in stock. None of the three answered The Post’s questions or explained why they are not recorded as having contributed to the ballroom fundraising campaign. Neither did the Trust for the National Mall or the White House. Kevin Crowe, Samantha Schmidt, Dan Lamothe and Alex Horton contributed to this report. - - - Graphics: Donations by date Major donors Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/investigations/2026/10/15/secret-documents-reveal-donors-behind-330-million-trumps-ballroom/

item.title: An FBI arrest revives fears that U.S. tech companies are hiring spies
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
On paper, Abdulrahman Alfozan seemed like an ideal candidate for one of Silicon Valley's most coveted artificial intelligence jobs. The Saudi national attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and landed an engineering job at Meta, according to his LinkedIn page and online records. Alfozan later secured a green card, spoke enthusiastically on a podcast about his Silicon Valley career and was invited to speak at Stanford University, all while working as a part-time partner at a venture capital fund dedicated to expanding the tech ecosystem in the Middle East. He had lived in the United States for more than a decade when he scored a mid-level role at OpenAI last year. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But Alfozan's arrest on Tuesday for allegedly planting a recording device in OpenAI's headquarters has ignited a fierce debate about the potential risks of Silicon Valley's international workforce - employees who often hail from nations seeking to rival the AI superpower status of the U.S. Foreign nationals have long formed the backbone of the American tech industry, helping U.S. companies surpass their would-be international rivals. Last week, President Donald Trump awarded national medals to six tech titans for their contributions to American innovation. Five of them, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, were immigrants. As countries battle to dominate AI, some top executives in Silicon Valley have argued that winning what they see as an existential arms race requires aggressively recruiting even more top talent from around the world. As recently as April, Katrina Mulligan, a senior member of OpenAI's national security team, called for an "accelerated pathway to citizenship" for such workers, referring to foreign hires as a "national strategic asset" at an event on Capitol Hill. She estimated that a significant number of OpenAI's employees were not U.S. citizens, including Chinese nationals. Just half of the 300 top AI researchers in the world, she said, were American. Other industry leaders - as well as some lawmakers - have long accused top-tier tech companies with many foreign workers of disadvantaging Americans and being breeding grounds for Chinese espionage. Palmer Luckey, CEO of weapons maker Anduril, and venture capitalist Shaun Maguire of Sequoia Capital took to X on Wednesday to revisit arguments that the industry should focus on hiring U.S. citizens. "Silicon Valley has operated with maximum openness and maximum naivete toward foreign tradecraft," Maguire wrote. Alfozan's arrest and the debates it has re-ignited show how the AI boom has sharpened a fundamental tension in Silicon Valley: American firms must recruit from a global pool of talent while also protecting innovations that governments around the world are racing to develop or obtain for themselves. The situation is getting even more complicated as competition intensifies, said Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, and a member of the National Security Council during the Biden administration. "This technology is too powerful for [countries beyond the U.S. and China] to ignore, and the quickest and cheapest way to advance capabilities is to steal it," he added. Arrests and convictions are relatively rare compared to the large numbers of foreign workers at U.S. tech firms. Much discussion focuses on workers from China, whose government has pledged to overtake the U.S. in AI. American intelligence agencies have long warned U.S. tech firms that they are targets of Chinese intelligence services. "There are any number of countries that would want to know about the internal workings and future plans of OpenAI and its competitors," said Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a Washington think tank. A spokesperson for OpenAI declined to comment. The company said in a statement late Tuesday that Alfozan's employment had been terminated. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) In recent years, the Middle East has sought to become a major force in American technology. Funding from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia have helped to fuel the costly AI boom, and billion-dollar investments often come with reciprocal obligations for U.S. AI companies to build advanced tech in the region. Last year the Trump administration gave both countries access to some of the most advanced AI chips in the U.S. - reversing the Biden administration's more cautious stance. Alfozan has not been charged with foreign espionage and the U.S. government has not said whether he was acting alone or as an agent of a foreign government. But there are signs that the U.S. government is exploring the latter possibility, McGuire said. The Department of Justice's press release about the incident says that the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control section, whose responsibility includes prosecuting spies, is assisting with the case. National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, in his statements on the case, said U.S. intelligence was committed to protecting America from "foreign threats." A Washington-based Middle East expert, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid incurring wrath from Saudi Arabia, said he believed the Saudi government was almost certainly involved in some way. "No one does this, not even for patriotism, without getting paid," said the person. And money would not be distributed without agreement by the Saudi royal court, he said. The Saudis lag behind their regional rival, the United Arab Emirates, in artificial intelligence development, he added. A former CIA officer with extensive experience in the Middle East, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal Saudi dynamics, said that Saudi nationals working in Silicon Valley are celebrated back home. It's a "huge thing" for the Saudi government, said the former agency official, because Riyadh wants to build its own native technology talent base. By working at a prominent Silicon Valley firm, you become a "big dog," said the former officer. Alfozan, his wife and a third family member had booked one-way tickets to travel on Oct. 12 from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul, according to a motion filed by the government Oct. 8 in federal court and unsealed Wednesday. The former OpenAI employee's public biography shows links to the Saudi government. Prince Khalid bin Bader al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, is a partner at RAED Ventures, which also lists Alfozan as a partner. The firm's X account has posted photos of partners hosting several high-ranking Saudi officials at events. RAED did not respond to a request for comment. In a podcast interview posted last month, Alfozan said he met Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, before he became the country's top leader during one of the prince's trips to Silicon Valley. Bin Salman inspired Alfozan to stay in Silicon Valley and grow his skills so that he could use them when he eventually returned to Saudi Arabia, he said in the interview. At OpenAI on Wednesday, employees continued tense conversations about the political implications of the arrest for immigrant workers, two OpenAI employees said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe internal discussions. The Justice Department said Tuesday that OpenAI determined the device was likely planted on Sept. 28. A company spokesman said it was found in a security sweep two days later. The arrest triggered a discussion on OpenAI's internal Slack messaging platform among employees about whether the incident might increase pressure from the Trump administration on OpenAI to not hire foreign nationals, said one of the people. In March, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer, wrote in court papers that AI developer Anthropic's reliance on staff with ties to China was among the concerns that fueled the Defense Department's conflict with the AI company. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. Lawmakers have been seeking to tighten the government's oversight of the security risks faced by AI companies. In September, Sens. Jim Banks (R-Indiana) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York) introduced a bill that would require AI companies that do business with the Pentagon to tell officials how they vet personnel and manage threats posed by insiders, and to report incidents of suspected espionage. "While we await more details, this incident underscores the need for a commonsense notification framework for AI contractors to alert the Pentagon to a range of security threats," Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday. Tensions inside the tech industry over hiring and security practices spilled out openly Wednesday on X. Silicon Valley insiders recounted stories of stiff security within tech firms due to concerns about espionage from both commercial companies and foreign governments, in recent years. Many companies have stepped up their security practices during the recent AI boom, often using the technology itself to speed up their understanding of strange behavior and patterns, according to Ryan Schonfeld, cofounder and CEO of HiveWatch, a startup that helps tech companies secure their facilities against insider threats. "What used to be considered very sophisticated ... now is par for the course," he said. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/fbi-arrest-revives-fears-u-090000730.html

item.title: Could this be the year Democrats close the 'governor gap' with Republicans?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
When people talk about this year's midterms, they tend to focus on whether Democrats will end unified Republican control of Congress by winning the U.S. Senate or House of Representatives (or both). And that makes sense: Congress has the power to check President Trump's agenda, so the national repercussions could be huge. But on Election Day, there will be something else to watch out for: whether Democrats can emerge with more governors' mansions than Republicans. GOP governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). That's given Republicans more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and build executive experience. But this year, Democrats have a real shot at closing the "governor gap." They need to net one governorship to tie Republicans at 25; net two, and they'll secure a gubernatorial "majority" for the first time since 2011. At the moment, 16 of this year's 36 gubernatorial contests are considered competitive, according to the expert race handicappers at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report — and 11 of them are in Republican-held states. So Democrats are on offense. It remains to be seen, however, whether they will actually overcome decades of GOP gubernatorial dominance in places like Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas on Nov. 3. Here are the races to watch. Alaska Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Bernadette Wilson. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Becky Bohrer/AP Party control: GOP The Republican: Bernadette Wilson The Democrat: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins Alaska hasn't elected a Democratic governor in 28 years. But that could change on Nov. 3 as Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins — known locally as JKT — has emerged as the frontrunner to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. In part, that's due to the Last Frontier's unique voting system, which sends the top four primary candidates to the general election regardless of party — then asks voters to rank them on Election Day in order of preference, from first to fourth. As a result, Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former state representative, is the only Democrat competing against three Republicans: conservative activist Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former state Attorney General Treg Taylor. Yahoo But economic dissatisfaction, Trump's low approval ratings in the state and Kreiss-Tomkins's energetic campaign are also helping to boost Democratic hopes. Recent polls suggest Kreiss-Tomkins could win the first round of ranked-choice balloting with nearly 50% of the vote — roughly twice as much as the second-place candidate (Wilson). On Oct. 13, Cook shifted its race rating from "toss up" to "lean Democrat." Along with Iowa, the outlet wrote, Alaska "may be Democrats' best opportunity to flip a governors' mansion in a red state." Florida David Jolly and Byron Donalds. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Rebecca Blackwell/AP, Alex Wong/Getty Images Party control: GOP The Republican: Byron Donalds The Democrat: David Jolly A former swing state, Florida has trended increasingly Republican during the Trump era. The governor's mansion, however, has been red ever since Jeb Bush won the job in 1998. U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds — the third Black Republican in history to represent the Sunshine State on Capitol Hill — is seeking to keep the GOP's streak alive by succeeding term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. His opponent is Democrat David Jolly , a former Republican congressman who left the GOP during Trump's first term. The president endorsed Donalds, a staunch social conservative, before he even entered the race; in Congress, Donalds has closely aligned himself with Trump's MAGA policies , especially on immigration. Meanwhile, Jolly is emphasizing his Christian faith, his conversion from Republican to independent to Democrat and his approach to key local issues like homeowner's insurance (which involves creating a state-backed catastrophe fund to keep costs down). Recent polls mostly show Donalds — who has raised more than seven times as much money as Jolly — leading by single-digit margins, with less than 50% of the vote; a few suggest a tie. Cook rates the race as "lean Republican." Georgia Keisha Lance Bottoms and Rick Jackson. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Megan Varner/Getty Images, Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images Party control: GOP The Republican: Rick Jackson The Democrat: Keisha Lance Bottoms Georgia has become the purplest of purple states in recent years: Trump lost it by 0.2 percentage points in 2020 and won it by 2 points in 2024. But while Georgians have sent two Democrats to the U.S. Senate in recent years — Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff — they haven't elected a Democratic governor since 1998. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has a chance to break the pattern on Nov. 3. The polls show her within striking distance — anywhere from 1 to 3 percentage points — of health care billionaire Rick Jackson, who won the GOP nomination without Trump's endorsement. Both candidates are promising to lower the cost of living by lowering taxes — a mainstream message in a relatively centrist state. Jackson has a huge financial edge , but Cook still rates the race as a toss up. If elected, Bottoms would make history as Georgia's first woman governor and the first Black woman governor anywhere in the U.S. Iowa Rob Sand and Zach Lahn. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Scott Olson/Getty Images, Anna Moneymaker/AP Party control: GOP The Republican: Zach Lahn The Democrat: Rob Sand Iowa is another state that hasn't elected a Democratic governor in decades — 20 years to be exact. But state auditor Rob Sand, 44, has led in every poll conducted this cycle , often by double-digit margins. As auditor — and before that, as Iowa's assistant attorney general — Sand developed a reputation as a "happy warrior for nonpartisan technocratic efficiency and anti-corruption," a leading progressive activist recently told the Atlantic . He has also downplayed his allegiance to the national Democratic Party, calling it "the lesser of two evils." Such positioning has made Sand perhaps the most popular politician in a state where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by almost 200,000. Sand's opponent, businessman Zach Lahn, narrowly upset Trump's pick, Rep. Randy Feenstra, in this summer's Republican primary. A Kansas resident until 2023, Lahn has struggled to overcome accusations of carpetbagging ever since. Cook says the race "leans Democrat" and describes it as the party's best pickup opportunity. Kansas Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Mark Reinstein/MediaPunch /IPX Party control: Democratic The Republican: Ty Masterson The Democrat: Cindy Holscher Kansas is anything but a blue state; since 1940, it has voted Republican in every presidential election but one — Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide. But the Sunflower State has elected two Democratic women governors in recent years: Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027). State Sen. Cindy Holscher is seeking to become the third. Holscher has her work cut out for her, though. She's up against Ty Masterson, the president of the state Senate, who leads by a few percentage points in most recent polls . Cook rates the Kansas contest as "lean Republican," making it this year's only potential blue-to-red flip with that rating. If Masterson does win in November, it wouldn't be particularly surprising. Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's mansion for longer than eight consecutive years. Nevada Aaron Ford and Joe Lombardo. Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: David Becker/AP, John Locher/AP Party control: GOP The Republican: Joe Lombardo The Democrat: Aaron Ford Incumbent GOP Gov. Joe Lombardo — the former sheriff of Clark County — won in 2022 on a law-and-order message. But Nevada is a swing state, and Lombardo's insistence on vetoing a raft of affordability bills passed by the Democratic legislature — to cap the cost of prescription drugs; to provide paid family leave to workers; to prohibit private equity and big banks from buying up housing en masse; to continue universal free breakfast and lunch for K-12 schoolchildren — has become a source of criticism in a cycle often centered on the cost of living. And his previous support for data-center subsidies hasn't helped . Enter state Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running on his working-class roots . item.title: Fort Hood shooter will not be executed on livestream, Trump says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump said on Thursday that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing a plan announced by the Pentagon earlier this month. The Pentagon announced Oct. 5 that Trump had approved Hasan's execution by firing squad at Fort Hood. Pentagon officials subsequently told the Associated Press that the execution, due to take place on Dec. 3, would be livestreamed. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed." He said the execution "may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose." He said that streaming the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM," but added that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device." Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Texas military base. The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice on Oct. 8 that the execution would be "public." "He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Hegseth said. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." On Oct. 9, Trump had said he "absolutely" approved the livestream plan, later telling reporters, "We're looking at it." ABC News reported on Tuesday that some officials had "raised concerns about the optics of broadcasting an execution" and are worried that the footage could fuel anti-American propaganda, particularly among Islamic extremist groups. CNN also reported that Trump had privately remarked that he initially did not know Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down. Hasan sustained injuries that left him paralyzed during an exchange of gunfire with police in the 2009 attack. President Trump confirmed that Hasan's execution will not be livestreamed. Alex Wong via Getty Images Vice President JD Vance said, "I'm not going to be watching" a livestream of the execution, should it be broadcast live, while House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News that some colleagues "have concerns," among them the possibility the video "would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." Hasan exhausted his regular appeals in 2025. He could choose to challenge his execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution beyond the current administration. The U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights told the AFP news agency, "The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture." Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, carried out the mass shooting on Nov. 5, 2009 after walking into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, at Fort Hood near Killeen, Texas, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups. According to the Associated Press , Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides." Why a firing squad rather than lethal injection? The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change. The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June. Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah. Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods. Following the high-profile failure of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee on Sept. 30, several top Republicans in the state said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP , "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully." Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session. "We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point." How common are military executions? Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth. The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl. item.title: Wholesale inflation jumped last month by most in 4 years as gas prices soared
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Wholesale prices in September rose to their highest level in nearly four years, largely propelled by higher energy prices. The sharp increase stokes concerns that inflation could broaden and keep the Federal Reserve on watch for further rate hikes. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand, which measures the prices that factories, farmers, and producers charge for their finished goods and services, rose 6.3% last month, the largest increase since December 2022. The data trounced expectations for a 5.4% rise. On a "core" basis, excluding food and energy, PPI jumped 0.7% month over month in September, handily higher than market expectations of 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, this core measure jumped 5.0%, up from 4.7% previously "With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers , it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. "While we don't expect them to raise rates later this month because it is so close to the mid-term election , we do think that they will increase the Fed Funds rate another 25 bps in December," Zaccarelli added. Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to gasoline prices, which jumped 20.3%. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7%. Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation Looking into the supply chain, the increases in the price of goods sold by one business to another were broad-based, with the index for processed goods rising 2.5%, prices for unprocessed goods moving up 8.4%, and the index for services advancing 0.9%. The index for processed goods sold to other businesses rose 2.5%, the largest rise since jumping 2.8% in May — with most of the increase due to a 10% spike in energy prices. Nearly half of the rise in processed goods sold to other businesses is attributable to a 21% increase in diesel fuel prices . Wholesale prices act as an early-warning pipeline for inflation. If the prices of these input goods rise, manufacturers could pass those higher costs down to consumers later. Yahoo Finance In the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, four districts reported that the pace of price increases has picked up since September. Higher oil prices permeated all 12 Fed districts. Companies reported elevated diesel prices and noted that fuel surcharges were passing on increased costs throughout the supply chain. Businesses in multiple districts also noted continued price pressure from other commodities, tariffs, and insurance. Consumer-facing companies said their profit margins have tightened as price-sensitive customers continue to resist price hikes. Businesses are managing their margins with selective price hikes, targeted incentives, and menu changes that reduce their costs. The reading on wholesale prices for September comes a day after consumer prices also surprised to the upside. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% in September, compared with expectations for 3.6%, and an acceleration from 3.4% in August. Month-over-month prices rose 0.6%, versus expectations for 0.5%. Stripping out volatile food and energy prices — the way the Fed likes to scrutinize underlying inflation — CPI rose 0.3% month over month, compared with expectations for 0.2%, holding the same level as August. The year-over-year rate was 2.6%, compared with expectations for 2.5%, and up from 2.4% in August. Analysts will use PPI and CPI to back into the Fed's preferred inflation gauge – the core Personal Consumption Expenditures index. Stephen Brown, an economist at Capital Economics, estimates that core PCE rose 0.35% in September. "That makes an October rate hike a bit more likely, with the FOMC's decision coming down to developments in broader financial conditions in the next couple of weeks and whether Fed officials are happier to surprise the market under Chair Kevin Warsh than has typically been the case," Brown said. A motorist fills up the tank at a gas station in Riverwoods, Ill., on Oct. 14, 2026. (AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh) AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh On Thursday morning, markets were still pricing in only about a 30% chance of the Fed hiking rates in less than two weeks, with a better chance of a hike in December. Investors appear to be taking cues from guidance given earlier this month from Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams, who have tempered expectations for a rate hike later this month. Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but warning that the central bank should take time to watch and assess whether inflation will come down in a timely manner. Williams told Bloomberg on Tuesday that he still sees one more interest rate hike as appropriate this year, but doesn't believe the central bank will need to raise rates again in 2027. The minutes from the September meeting read that most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday that hotter-than-expected September consumer inflation was "discouraging" but suggested that he wants to wait for more data before further raising interest rates. He said core inflation remaining as high as it is now would not be "acceptable" nor "compatible with the Fed target, and our policy needs to address that." item.title: Trump admin. sues California over alleged noncitizens on state's voter rolls
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Andrew Goudsward and Luc Cohen WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department sued California on Thursday, asking a federal judge to block the state from counting mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are ‌likely noncitizens. The lawsuit marks the latest effort by President Donald Trump's administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the ‌midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress. The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to individual states, though the federal government ​has some oversight role. Trump has repeatedly claimed that voting by noncitizens - which is illegal - is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found that just 129 people had been prosecuted for noncitizen voting since the statute criminalizing it passed in 1996. The Justice Department has ramped up such prosecutions in recent months. In the lawsuit filed in federal court in Los Angeles, the Justice Department sought a court order preventing California from "tabulating in federal elections vote-by-mail ballots received" ‌from more than 20,000 voters until their immigration status is ⁠verified. Reuters previously reported that the department sent California a letter giving it a 48-hour deadline on Tuesday to review the list of alleged noncitizen voters. The list was provided on a thumb drive. CALIFORNIA SAYS DOJ SEEKS CHAOS The lawsuit marks an escalation ⁠in the federal government's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. The Justice Department has warned election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington DC for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters' ​sensitive ​personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one. In Thursday's ​lawsuit against California, the Justice Department said the Department of Homeland ‌Security had identified the 20,000 alleged noncitizens by comparing voter rolls to its own internal databases. Voting rights activists have expressed concern that many citizens who are naturalized could be wrongly flagged as noncitizens due to outdated DHS data. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, who were named as defendants in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a statement on Wednesday about the letter, Weber said California's safeguards against noncitizen voting were robust. "The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in ‌our elections," Weber said. NONCITIZENS HAVE BEEN REGISTERED THROUGH ERRORS Though states may have added more than ​30,000 noncitizens to their voter rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters ​found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. ​Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country’s 170 million registered voters to affect elections. Rick Hasen, a law ‌professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an expert ​on election law, said the DOJ’s request ​would potentially cause California to violate a federal law barring states from conducting mass purges of voter rolls within 90 days of an election. The Trump administration has argued in another case that such restrictions should not apply to removal of noncitizens because they were not legally authorized to ​register in the first place. Hasen said the DOJ lawsuit would ‌likely face legal hurdles. “The federal government doesn’t have any business directly telling states what ballots they can or cannot send out or ​not count,” he said. “I just don’t see the federal authority to do that over a state.” (Reporting by Andrew Goudsward in Washington and Luc ​Cohen in New York; Editing by Michelle Nichols, Matthew Lewis and David Gregorio) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/doj-sues-california-block-votes-171601356.html

item.title: GOP questions the accuracy of polling leading up to the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans nervous about the midterms are increasingly turning to the same salve: The polling will be wrong. They aren't suggesting Republicans will have a good night come Nov. 3 — or that the party will hold the House. But they're clinging to the possibility that it could be a typically bad midterm year reminiscent of 2022, when polls projected Democrats would be pummeled, only for those predictions to fall short. It's happened in other cycles, too, they note. President Donald Trump outperformed final polling averages in all seven swing states in 2024 and defied the national polls in 2016 as well. This story is based on conversations with more than a dozen people, including veteran GOP operatives, pollsters, strategists working on battleground races and national party officials. Most conceded the national environment is bad for Republicans and has only gotten worse over the last few months. But even a small sampling error, they say, could completely change how election night turns out for the GOP. "Part of the challenge here is polling still has not figured out how to model Republican voters who either don't answer the phone or just aren't really interested in polling, and so I do think that the Senate map across the board, there's more reason to doubt the polls than you would guess by seeing how both media and Democrats are treating this," said Matt Whitlock, a GOP strategist and former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser. Republicans' growing reliance on bad polling to ease their pain reflects the dour mood gripping the party. With less than three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are increasingly pessimistic about their prospects, as persistent inflation, high prices on everyday items, elevated mortgage rates and a lingering war in the Middle East hamper campaigns. On Wednesday, the Labor Department reported inflation accelerated more than expected in September driven by soaring gas prices, the latest blow to Republicans who are facing voters' ire over cost-of-living concerns. And this week, top Republican super PACs aligned with Trump and congressional Republican leadership pulled money from a handful of GOP House members seeking reelection. Senior House Republicans have privately concluded that the chamber is all but gone and party leaders are shifting resources to save the Senate. Both the White House and RNC said polls have sold short GOP support. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said "underestimating" Trump and his administration "have proven the experts and pollsters wrong every single time," while RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre added that "bed-wetting strategists who aren't in the game always take the bait." "Republicans are united in exposing the far-left's extreme agenda and will leave it all on the table to defy history in November," she said. But the polling, like the economic headwinds, has only worsened in recent weeks. Democrats hold a roughly 9-point national lead on the generic congressional ballot, up from about 6.5 points around Labor Day. That's slightly wider than the Democrats' lead at this point in 2018, when the party rode a blue wave to a 41-seat gain in the House. Senate seats in GOP strongholds such as Texas, Alaska, Iowa and Kansas are in play, as independent voters sour on the president and his policies. Still, GOP strategist Colin Reed said the polling industry is "very much in transition" and that making predictions in the Trump era is a "risky gambit." GOP pollster Patrick Ruffini, co-founder of Echelon Insights, found that in three Midwestern states — Iowa, Michigan and Ohio — 93 percent of Senate polls overestimated the Democratic candidate's performance. In both midterm and presidential election years, polls a month out from the election were off by an average of more than 6 points in Democrats' favor. "We can get the environment right, but the map wrong," Ruffini said. "Even if you buy this idea of a Democratic wave, a good Democratic year, a very solidly pro-Democratic environment, we should be concerned about the track record of the polls — particularly in some of these red states where there have been some pretty large misses, and especially in the Midwest." Part of the challenge is no one knows what the midterm electorate will look like, making it hard to know if the polling is accurate. A White House official, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly, said they didn't think that Black voters would show up for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, but it's unclear whether that means they vote for Republican Mike Rogers — or just stay home. "There is a narrative building process in all of these different polls," the official said, adding that "it's different in every state. There's not a one size fits all. Whenever you look at which poll is overweighting which subset of voters, they're all over the place." That's partly why Trump is appearing in red states — to shape the electorate and make sure it's reflective of the MAGA coalition that carried him to victory in 2024. Multiple GOP strategists pointed to 2022 when Democrats outperformed expectations and held the Senate, even as they lost the House. The Biden White House, even with the loss of the lower chamber, took a victory lap, celebrating the better-than-expected election night as a "good day." "Republicans' only hope in '26 is that what happened to us in '22 happens to Democrats in '26," said a GOP strategist working on battleground races. "There's a part of me that thinks there is a scenario where 2022 repeats itself. But if the polling is right … then I think it's setting up to be one of the worst cycles in history for Republicans." Polling over the last decade has struggled to capture Republican voters. The data underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024, and Republicans argue similar errors could be happening again this cycle, particularly in competitive Senate races. "Polling is getting much more difficult to do," said veteran GOP strategist Karl Rove, adding that if the polls reflect Democratic overperformance "then every one of these races that we're talking about today — Texas, Michigan, Maine, Alaska, Iowa — they're all within the margin of error." An RNC official argued that public polls skew toward Democrats. "It's not to say that the environment's wildly different from what we anticipated it was going to be, which is a tough one in a midterm, which is what history tells you a midterm environment is going to be," the person said. "I think generally speaking, the polls are far more pessimistic than the reality is for Republicans in the midterms." Text polling has skewed the responses because it overpresents young liberal voters and progressives, especially in states that have a large white population, as many of the Great Plains states do, said a second GOP strategist working on competitive midterm races. Pollsters try to balance their samples but can only do so much to correct for that. The strategist also noted that the polling right now reflects a change in the electorate as profound as those seen after Watergate and 9/11. "It would be so historically unprecedented you'd have to presuppose we're staring down the barrel of a generational national trauma that no one is aware of," the strategist said. Adam Wren contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/republicans-last-hope-2026-another-090000613.html

item.title: Trump says he's 'very proud' as he unveils newly renovated White House facade
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has shared new images of what he described as the “fully renovated” White House facade, saying extensive restoration work has given the historic building decades of additional life. Trump posted photographs of the South side of the White House to Truth Social early Thursday, highlighting restoration of the exterior as well as a new South Entrance and helipad. “Actual pictures of our fully renovated White House facade, facing South, with the new South Entrance, and Heliport!” Trump wrote. “It had to be done, and I am very proud to be the President who did it!” Trump added. President Donald Trump is seen on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., on September 26, 2026. The work comes amid a much broader transformation of the White House complex during Trump’s second term, including work on the North Portico, changes to the Rose Garden and extensive construction on the site of the former East Wing for a new ballroom and military complex. Trump said Thursday that the ballroom and military complex were “on time, and on budget,” describing them as an “unbelievably beautiful addition” to the White House. The project has been the subject of legal challenges and scrutiny over its cost and funding, with the Supreme Court allowing construction to continue in August while litigation over the project proceeds. Newsweek has contacted the White House and National Park Service for further comment. The South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, as seen March 20, 2009. What Changed at the White House? Trump’s newly released photographs focus on the South facade, one of the most recognizable views of the White House. The South Portico, with its curved colonnade and Truman Balcony above it, faces the South Lawn and has historically served as an arrival and departure point for presidents and foreign leaders. Trump said the work addressed deterioration to both the building’s exterior walls and decorative architectural features. “Over the years, the facade, both North and South, suffered tremendous wear, tear, and damage,” he wrote. “The exterior walls and ornamentation, both missing and in bad condition, has been fully restored to the Highest Level, giving the White House many decades of additional life!” The president did not provide a detailed breakdown of the restoration work or its cost. Work has also been underway on the White House’s North Portico. The Washington Post reported in September that workers had spent roughly two months repairing the historic columns and strengthening the entrance before coverings surrounding the structure began to be removed. The White House itself dates to the 1790s, although the building has repeatedly been rebuilt, expanded and renovated. The South Portico was constructed during James Monroe’s presidency in the 1820s, while the North Portico was added several years later under Andrew Jackson. The West Wing was constructed during Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency in 1902 and the White House underwent a near-total interior reconstruction during Harry Truman’s presidency between 1948 and 1952. An image posted on Truth Social shows the newly renovated White House facade. Trump’s White House Renovations The facade restoration is part of a series of changes Trump has made to the White House and its grounds, among the most significant being the ballroom and associated East Wing redevelopment. The original East Wing was demolished as the administration moved ahead with plans for a large new ceremonial space and additional security and military infrastructure. Trump initially promoted the ballroom as a privately funded addition designed to give the White House a permanent space for large state events rather than relying on temporary tents. The project has since expanded to include substantial underground security infrastructure and other facilities. In August, the Supreme Court permitted construction to continue while a lawsuit brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation proceeds. The Court said its ruling did not decide the ultimate legality of the project but found that the government was likely to prevail on its argument that the preservation group lacked standing. Trump has repeatedly said taxpayers will not pay for the ballroom itself. In September, he said the ballroom would cost close to $400 million and was being funded by himself and private companies. Internal contractor documents reported by The Washington Post , however, estimated the wider East Wing project at about $600 million, with approximately $293 million expected from private sources and the remainder associated with government-funded security, military and Executive Residence work. The White House has said those taxpayer-funded costs relate to security and other government functions rather than the ballroom itself. Trump reiterated Thursday that the work remained on schedule. “Likewise, the Ballroom and Military Complex, is on time, and on budget,” he wrote. Trump said the development would be the most significant addition to the White House since the West Wing was constructed. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Tobias Meyjes and Tony Phillips . item.title: Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway. George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base. CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels. The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks. The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. "Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge." An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years. CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026. The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs. Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production. In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year. While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages. One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels. Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops." He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing." "Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests." How munitions are used around the world The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge. Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world. The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long. The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons. But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address. For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China. There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen. What led to the current weapons systems shortage? After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian. "After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories." He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did." The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis. Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting. Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production. "We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict." Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries. Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War. Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.
